questions.q:
In July 2026 the Governor of Karnataka suspended the Chairperson of the Karnataka Public Service Commission under Article 317(2), pending a reference to the Supreme Court. Consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 317(2), a Governor can suspend the Chairman or a member of a State Public Service Commission pending the Supreme Court's report on a reference.
2. A State Public Service Commission Chairman can be removed for misbehaviour by the Governor after an inquiry by the State High Court.
3. A Chairman or member of a State Public Service Commission is removed by the President, and not by the Governor, on the ground of misbehaviour found by the Supreme Court on a reference.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Under Article 317, the removal of even a State PSC member is done by the President, after the Supreme Court (on a reference) reports misbehaviour; the Governor's role is limited to suspension pending that inquiry. Statement 2 gets both the removing authority (President) and the inquiring body (Supreme Court, not the High Court) wrong.
questions.h: Governor suspends, President removes, Supreme Court inquires

questions.q:
In Dr. Abdul Hameed v. State of Rajasthan (21 July 2026), the Supreme Court set aside the conviction and death sentence in the 1996 Samleti (Dausa) bus-blast case and ordered a fresh trial because the accused had been denied effective legal representation. Consider the following statements:
1. Article 39A, a Directive Principle added by the 42nd Amendment, directs the State to secure equal justice and free legal aid.
2. Article 22(1) gives a person who is arrested the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.
3. Article 39A is a Fundamental Right and is therefore directly enforceable against the State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Free legal aid flows from three provisions: Article 21 (fair trial), Article 22(1) (counsel of choice for the arrested) and Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid). Article 39A sits in Part IV as a Directive Principle, not in Part III, so it is not directly enforceable by itself; courts enforce it by reading it into Article 21.

questions.q: In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (July 2026), a Supreme Court bench directed all States and Union Territories to frame and notify, within three months, a policy for early or premature release of elderly and terminally ill prisoners. The direction is addressed to the States and UTs mainly because
o: prisons fall in the Union List, and States act only as agents of the Union in running them
'Prisons, reformatories and Borstal institutions' is an entry in the Concurrent List, so each State must frame a uniform policy
'Prisons, reformatories, Borstal institutions and other institutions of a like nature' is an entry in the State List, so release policy is primarily a State matter
the power of remission of sentences under Article 72 is exercised by the President on the advice of State Governments
questions.e: Prisons and the persons detained in them are Entry 4 of the State List, so States run the jails and frame release and remission policies (the Governor's power under Article 161 also operates at State level). The Court therefore directed every State and UT to notify its own policy rather than ordering a single Union scheme. Entry 4 is not in the Union or Concurrent List.

questions.q: On 20 July 2026 the Supreme Court (Abhishek Baxi & Others v. Union of India) directed the Centre and CBSE to apply nationwide a direction giving parents an express opt-out in the consent form for APAAR, the education ID linked to a child's Aadhaar. The direction being extended nationwide was originally issued by the
questions.e: The Court extended the Orissa High Court's direction on an express parental opt-out across the country, and also restricted third-party sharing of student data. APAAR (Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry) is the 'One Nation One Student ID' under NEP 2020, so the case sits at the intersection of education policy and the privacy right under Article 21.

questions.q:
By a notification dated 23 July 2026 amending the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs was split into two departments. Consider the following statements:
1. The Department of Capital Development was created to handle Delhi-related matters such as CPWD, DDA and the Delhi Metro.
2. The Allocation of Business Rules are made by the President under Article 77(3) of the Constitution.
3. The Department of Capital Development was assigned national urban schemes such as Swachh Bharat Mission, AMRUT and PM SVANidhi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 77(3) empowers the President to make rules for the allocation of business among Ministers and for the convenient transaction of Government business, so a Ministry can be restructured by amending these Rules without any law. In this split the national schemes (SBM, AMRUT, PM SVANidhi) went to the Department of Urban Development, while Delhi-specific bodies went to Capital Development; statement 3 swaps them.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ministry of Cooperation, which marked its 5th Foundation Day on 6 July 2026:
1. It was created on 6 July 2021 by carving it out of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare.
2. The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 added Part IXB on cooperative societies and Article 43B as a Directive Principle.
3. 'Cooperative societies' is a subject in the Union List of the Seventh Schedule.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Ministry was carved out of Agriculture, and the 97th Amendment inserted Part IXB and Article 43B (and also made the right to form cooperatives a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c)). Cooperative societies are Entry 32 of the State List, not the Union List, which is why the Centre works through a Ministry, funds and model laws rather than direct legislation for State cooperatives.

questions.q:
Statement-I: A Delhi High Court bench ruled on 1 July 2026 that private media houses perform a 'public function', so a writ petition can lie against them in a High Court for violating an individual's right to privacy.
Statement-II: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and Article 226 writs lie only against the State and its instrumentalities.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct as reported. Statement-II is incorrect on both counts: under Article 226 a High Court can issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights 'and for any other purpose', which makes it wider than the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction, and writs can reach private bodies discharging public functions, which is the very reasoning of the ruling.
questions.s: The Indian Express via Anantam IAS, 6 Jul 2026
questions.h: 226 = Fundamental Rights AND any other purpose

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Census 2027 exercise:
1. The population-enumeration pre-test (rehearsal) held from 1 to 20 July 2026 covered all States and Union Territories.
2. The pre-test included a self-enumeration window from 1 to 5 July and recorded caste in a free-text 'open column', with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes on pre-assigned codes.
3. Census is an Entry in the Union List of the Seventh Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The pre-test ran in 16 States and Union Territories, not all of them, so statement 1 is wrong; a pre-test is a limited trial of forms, apps and procedures before the actual count. Census (Entry 69) is a Union subject, and the exercise runs under the Census Act, 1948.
questions.s: The Hindu via Anantam IAS, 7 Jul 2026

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about two Bills passed by Parliament in the Monsoon Session of 2026:
1. The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 was cleared by the Rajya Sabha on 29 July and by the Lok Sabha on 30 July 2026.
2. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 extends the criminal penalties of the 1971 Act to the National Song, Vande Mataram.
3. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 29 July and by the Lok Sabha on 30 July 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The order was reversed for the two Bills. The Public Examinations Amendment Bill went through the Lok Sabha (29 July, voice vote) first and then the Rajya Sabha (30 July), with Presidential assent on 31 July; the National Honour Bill started in the Rajya Sabha (29 July) and cleared the Lok Sabha on 30 July. A Bill becomes law only after both Houses pass it and the President assents.

questions.q:
On 5 August 2026 Parliament cleared the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, raising the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges, including the Chief Justice of India. Consider the following statements:
1. Article 124(1) leaves it to Parliament to fix, by law, the number of judges of the Supreme Court other than the Chief Justice.
2. The revised sanctioned strength of 38 includes the Chief Justice of India.
3. Increasing the number of Supreme Court judges requires a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368 passed by a special majority.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Parliament can change the strength of the Supreme Court by an ordinary law (here an amendment to the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956), because Article 124(1) says the Court consists of the Chief Justice and such number of other judges as Parliament may prescribe. The new figure of 38 includes the CJI. No Article 368 amendment is needed.

questions.q: Parliament passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 (Lok Sabha on 11 August, Rajya Sabha on 12 August 2026), renaming the State of Kerala as Keralam. Which one of the following statements about the procedure for altering the name of a State is NOT correct?
o: A Bill for the purpose can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of the President
The President is bound to accept the views expressed by the State Legislature when it is referred the draft Bill
Such a law can be passed by a simple majority and amends the First Schedule
Such a law is not treated as a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368
questions.e: Under Article 3 the President must refer the draft Bill to the State Legislature for its views, but he and Parliament are not bound by them (even a unanimous Assembly resolution, as in Kerala, is only a view). The law is passed by a simple majority and Article 4 says it is not an amendment under Article 368. That is why the Centre, not the State, has the final say in reorganising States.
questions.h: Article 3: State's view is heard, not obeyed

questions.q:
The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, passed by Parliament on 11 August 2026, creates a National Tribunals Commission and replaces the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021. Consider the following statements:
1. The National Tribunals Commission is to be chaired by a serving Supreme Court Judge.
2. The Bill replaces the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which had been partly struck down by the Supreme Court.
3. Article 323A allows State Legislatures to establish administrative tribunals for matters relating to the service conditions of State employees.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The Commission is chaired by a former Supreme Court Judge or a former High Court Chief Justice, not a serving judge, so statement 1 is wrong. Under Article 323A (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) only Parliament can create administrative tribunals for public service matters; Article 323B lets Parliament or State Legislatures set up tribunals for subjects such as taxation and land reforms.

questions.q:
Statement-I: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 (passed on 12-13 August 2026) inserts a Section 9D that bars State Governments from levying any tax, cess or other levy on mineral rights or mineral-bearing land except under conditions prescribed by the Centre.
Statement-II: Entry 50 of the State List allows States to tax mineral rights, but makes this power subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Entry 50 of the State List itself says that the State's power to tax mineral rights is 'subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development'. Parliament, using its power over mines and mineral development in the Union List (Entry 54), is therefore constitutionally entitled to cap the States' levies, which is what the new Section 9D does.
questions.h: Entry 50 (State): tax on minerals, but Parliament may limit

questions.q:
Match List-I (Bill passed by Parliament in August 2026) with List-II (key provision):
List-I
A. Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026
B. Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026
C. Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026
D. Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026
List-II
1. Order of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class needed for registering a birth or death delayed by more than two years
2. Statutory footing for the Udyam Registration Portal as a free, voluntary digital registration platform
3. Repeals the 1891 Act and recognises electronic, digital and cloud-based bank records as admissible evidence
4. Creates a National Tribunals Commission
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.e: Each Bill maps to one headline feature: late registration of births and deaths (JMFC order beyond two years), a statutory Udyam Portal for MSMEs, admissibility of electronic bank records under the new Bankers' Books Evidence law, and a National Tribunals Commission. A common trap is to mix the two 'registration' items, the births Bill and the Udyam registration.
questions.s: All India Radio and Business Standard, 4-11 Aug 2026

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Monsoon Session of Parliament 2026:
1. The Session began on 20 July 2026 and both Houses were adjourned sine die on 13 August 2026.
2. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses in the Session.
3. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 12 August and by the Rajya Sabha on 13 August 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026 (seeking a 'Designated Authority' to control assets linked to foreign contributions received by NGOs) was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee instead of being passed. A JPC is an ad hoc committee with members from both Houses; sending a Bill to it delays passage until the Committee reports.
questions.s: Business Standard and PRS India, 13 Aug 2026

questions.q: Which one of the following Bills was NOT passed by Parliament in the Monsoon Session of 2026 and was left pending at the end of the Session?
questions.e: The Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 (to replace the ISI Act, 1959 and convert the Institute from a registered society into a statutory body corporate) was the one Bill left pending. The NCDC (Amendment) Bill, the Kerala name Bill and the Tribunals Reforms Bill were all passed.

questions.q:
In Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab (September 2026), the Supreme Court held that arrest without communicating the grounds of arrest violates Article 22(1) and entitles the accused to release, and that re-arrest after such release requires prior judicial approval. Consider the following statements:
1. Article 22(1) requires that a person arrested be informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest.
2. The Court held that release for violation of Article 22(1) bars any re-arrest of the accused in all circumstances.
3. Under Article 22(2), an arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the journey time.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Court did not bar re-arrest altogether; it required prior judicial approval for it, and it distinguished release from unconstitutional detention from release on bail. Article 22(1) (grounds of arrest and counsel of choice) and 22(2) (production before a magistrate within 24 hours) are the core safeguards for an arrested person.

questions.q:
On 1 September 2026 the Supreme Court used its Article 142 powers to quash FIRs arising from the July 2026 NEET-UG protests and directed a pan-India compensation framework for protesters. Consider the following statements about Article 142:
1. It enables the Supreme Court to pass such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.
2. An order made under it is enforceable throughout the territory of India in the manner prescribed by or under law made by Parliament.
3. High Courts also have the same power under Article 142 in matters pending before them.
4. The Court used it in this case to quash FIRs and extend relief to similar cases in other States and Union Territories.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 142 is a special power of the Supreme Court alone; High Courts rely on Article 226 and their inherent powers instead, so statement 3 is wrong. The Court used the 'complete justice' power to reach FIRs even in other States, and its orders are enforceable across India.

questions.q:
On 18 September 2026 the Karnataka Cabinet approved Tulu as an additional (second) official administrative language for use in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts. Consider the following statements:
1. Article 345 allows the Legislature of a State to adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the State as the official language(s) of that State.
2. Tulu is included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
3. The Cabinet decision gives Tulu the status of an additional official administrative language in two districts of Karnataka.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 345 lets a State adopt one or more languages in use in the State (or Hindi) as official language, so the State can add Tulu for administrative use without any change in the Constitution. Tulu is not in the Eighth Schedule, which lists 22 languages, and such listing is a separate process that would bring it recognition by the Union.

questions.q: On 17 September 2026 the Election Commission of India froze the name and symbol of the All India Trinamool Congress and allotted separate names and symbols to two rival factions for two Assembly bypolls. A dispute between rival groups of a recognised political party, each claiming to be that party and its symbol, is decided by the Election Commission under
o: the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution
Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968
questions.e: Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968 empowers the Commission to decide rival claims within a recognised party and, pending that, to freeze the symbol. The Tenth Schedule deals with disqualification of legislators for defection (decided by the Presiding Officer), and Section 29A deals with registration of parties, not splits.

questions.q:
Tamil Nadu withdrew its 21 September 2026 Government Order that exempted the Public (Law and Order) Department from the Right to Information Act, 2005, after criticism. Consider the following statements:
1. Section 24(4) of the RTI Act allows a State Government to exempt, by notification, intelligence and security organisations established by it from the Act.
2. Even for such exempted organisations, information pertaining to allegations of corruption and human rights violations is not excluded from the Act.
3. A State Government may exempt any of its departments from the RTI Act by an executive Government Order without any notification under the Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Section 24(4) permits a State to notify its intelligence and security organisations as outside the Act, but the proviso keeps information on corruption and human rights violations within it. A whole Home or Law and Order Department is not such an organisation, and exemption must come through the Act's own route, which is why the order drew criticism and was withdrawn.

questions.q:
Bihar's Home Department notified in early September 2026 that prior State consent is mandatory for the CBI to investigate offences involving public servants of the Bihar Government, while general consent continues for Government of India employees. Consider the following statements:
1. The CBI derives its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.
2. Under Section 6 of that Act, the CBI needs the consent of the State Government to exercise its powers and jurisdiction in a State.
3. A High Court or the Supreme Court cannot direct a CBI investigation in a State without that State's consent.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The CBI is a creature of the DSPE Act, 1946, and Section 6 makes State consent necessary, so withdrawing or restricting general consent is a federal lever. Constitutional courts can, however, direct a CBI inquiry under Articles 32 and 226 without State consent, so statement 3 is wrong.

questions.q:
At talks with the Leh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance on 9 September 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs proposed a new Article 371(K) creating a directly elected Union-Territory-level body for Ladakh. Consider the following statements:
1. The Constitution at present contains special provisions for certain States only up to Article 371J.
2. Article 371A makes special provision for Nagaland and Article 371J for Karnataka.
3. A new Article 371(K) can be inserted by an executive order of the Ministry of Home Affairs without a Constitutional Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Articles 371 to 371J are the existing special provisions (371A Nagaland, 371J Karnataka's Hyderabad-Karnataka region). A new Article can only be added by a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368, so the Home Ministry's proposal would need Parliament's approval and not an executive notification.

questions.q:
The Union Home Ministry extended the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 by six more months in disturbed areas of Manipur and parts of Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh (September 2026). Consider the following statements:
1. An area can be declared 'disturbed' under Section 3 by the Governor of the State or by the Central Government.
2. Section 6 provides that no prosecution can be instituted against a person acting under the Act without the previous sanction of the State Government.
3. Section 4 powers can be exercised by a commissioned officer, a warrant officer, a non-commissioned officer or any other person of equivalent rank in the armed forces.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Section 6 requires the previous sanction of the Central Government (not the State Government) for prosecution of personnel acting under the Act, which is the legal basis of the protection that critics call immunity. Section 3 lets the Governor or the Centre declare an area disturbed, and Section 4 lists who can use the special powers.

questions.q: On 28 September 2026 the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly passed a resolution urging the Centre to restore full Statehood to Jammu and Kashmir, which has been a Union Territory since the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019. Restoring Statehood to the Union Territory would legally require
o: a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368 ratified by at least half of the State Legislatures
a law of Parliament under Article 3, passed by a simple majority, on the recommendation of the President
an Order of the President under Article 370 on the concurrence of the J&K Assembly
a resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly, which is binding on Parliament
questions.e: The J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 was an ordinary law under Article 3, and the same route (a law of Parliament, introduced on the President's recommendation) can restore Statehood. The Assembly's resolution is only a political request; under Article 3 even a State Legislature's views are not binding, and no Article 368 amendment is needed. Article 370 was already rendered inoperative in 2019.
